core: The ethical and practical foundation of confidentiality: candid disclosure and care depend on trust that information is protected
Privacy vs confidentiality vs security as three distinct but related concepts
Protected health information (PHI) and the minimum necessary principle, including the treatment exception
Permitted uses and disclosures at a conceptual level (treatment, payment, operations) and the role of authorization
Core patient rights over their information (access, amendment, accounting of disclosures, notice of privacy practices)
Special protections beyond baseline HIPAA: 42 CFR Part 2 for SUD records and stricter state laws
Everyday privacy practice in a healthcare setting (need-to-know, credentials, verbal privacy, disposal)
supporting: De-identified information is not PHI and can be used more freely
HIPAA is a floor; the more protective rule generally governs (preemption / more stringent)
outOfScope: The detailed HIPAA rule structure: Privacy Rule / Security Rule / Breach Notification Rule mechanics, covered entity and business associate machinery, enforcement and penalties (owned by HIPAA Foundations)
Records governance lifecycle and release-of-information mechanics (owned by Health Information Management)
EHR and security technical controls in depth (owned by Electronic Health Records)
Individualized legal, compliance, or benefits advice

claims.claim: Confidentiality is foundational because honest clinical disclosure, and therefore accurate diagnosis and effective care, depends on patients trusting that their information is protected; the HIPAA Privacy Rule's stated goal is to protect health information while allowing the flow of information needed for care and public health.

Privacy (the patient's right to control access), confidentiality (the duty of those entrusted to protect information), and security (the administrative, physical, and technical safeguards that enforce protection) are distinct concepts; HIPAA maps them roughly onto the Privacy Rule and Security Rule.

Protected health information is individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate in any form; identifiers tied to health information, including the fact that a person is a patient, are covered. Properly de-identified information is not PHI.

The minimum necessary principle requires reasonable efforts to limit use, disclosure, or request of PHI to the least needed for the purpose (45 CFR 164.502(b), 164.514(d)); it does not apply to disclosures to a health care provider for treatment.

A covered entity may use and disclose PHI without separate authorization for treatment, payment, and health care operations (45 CFR 164.506) and for defined public-purpose disclosures; other uses, such as most marketing or releasing psychotherapy notes, generally require the patient's written authorization (45 CFR 164.508).

Individuals have rights over their information including the right to inspect and obtain a copy (164.524), request an amendment (164.526), receive an accounting of disclosures (164.528), request restrictions and confidential communications (164.522), and receive a notice of privacy practices (164.520).

Substance use disorder treatment records from federally assisted programs receive heightened confidentiality under 42 CFR Part 2, historically requiring patient consent for many disclosures HIPAA would permit; a 2024 final rule (89 FR 12472, effective April 16, 2024, compliance February 16, 2026) aligned parts of Part 2 with HIPAA while preserving heightened protection.
HIPAA sets a national floor; where a state law is more stringent (more protective of privacy) it generally is not preempted and governs (45 CFR 160.202-160.203).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 42 CFR Part 2 still meaningfully differs from HIPAA after the 2024 final rule
positions: The 2024 rule aligned several Part 2 provisions (e.g., a single consent for TPO, HIPAA-style breach and enforcement) with HIPAA
Part 2 retains heightened protections, including restrictions on use in legal proceedings without consent or a court order
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that Part 2 was aligned in part while preserving heightened protection, which both positions support; it avoids asserting Part 2 is now identical to HIPAA.
